lines: Riley Chen
+1 (555) 010-7731 | riley.chen@example.com | example.com/in/riley-chen
EDUCATION
Northfield School of Management | MBA | Metro City, USA | Sep 2023 - Jun 2025
Lakeview University | B.A. in Economics | Lake City, USA | Sep 2014 - Jun 2018
EXPERIENCE
Coastal Marine Services | Diesel Mechanic | Lake City, USA | Jul 2025 - Present
- Rebuilt diesel engines and gearboxes for a fleet of 14 commercial fishing vessels, keeping dry-dock time under 5 days per job.
- Maintained hydraulic winch systems and logged service records for the harbor authority's annual inspections.
Crestline Logistics | Operations Analyst | Lake City, USA | Jul 2018 - Aug 2023
- Owned the weekly carrier scorecards for the regional managers and the monthly review meeting that discussed them.
- Cut warehouse pick errors 30% at two sites by redesigning slotting rules with the floor supervisors and retraining 45 pickers on the new layout.
- Ran the quarterly S&OP review across sales, finance and operations for 12 consecutive quarters, introducing a consensus forecast that cut forecast error from 18% to 11%.

- Led the rollout of a route-planning tool to 3 depots while rewriting the standard operating procedures, running driver training and taking over vendor negotiations for the telematics contract, which saved 1,800 driver hours a year across the region.
Harbor Payments | Associate Product Manager Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2024 - Aug 2024
- Redesigned merchant onboarding around a single verification step, cutting median time to first payment from 9 days to 4 across 2,300 new merchants in the pilot region.
- Lifted checkout conversion from 61% to 66% by testing a one-page flow against the three-step flow across 40,000 sessions, then shipping it to all merchants.
- Prioritized the dispute roadmap with RICE, scoring Reach as the number of support tickets each feature would close.
- After interviewing 25 merchants, mapping chargeback reasons, sizing the loss by segment and drafting a business case with finance, set the next quarter's roadmap priority.
- Ran the checkout A/B test with randomization by session and reported the 5-point conversion lift as the effect on merchants' customers.
- Presented the onboarding results and a follow-up roadmap to the payments leadership team, who funded the rollout to two more regions.
PROJECTS
Campus Food Rescue App | Product Lead | Student Venture | Oct 2023 - Present
- Launched a surplus-food pickup app to 3,100 students with two dining halls, redistributing 9 tonnes of food that would have been thrown away in its first year.
- Raised weekly active users from 400 to 1,150, a 150% increase, by adding pickup reminders chosen after 60 user interviews.
- Raised the pickup-slot fill rate by 20% across two dining halls, from 75% to 95%, by setting up a volunteer shift system.
MBA Consulting Practicum | Team Lead | Regional Hospital Network | Jan 2024 - May 2024
- Sized a $2.4M annual saving from consolidating outpatient scheduling across 4 clinics; the client funded a pilot based on the model.
- Patient intake at 4 clinics was mapped and the intake form was shortened, with the changes adopted by front-desk staff.
- Presented the final recommendation to the hospital COO and clinic directors, who approved a 90-day scheduling pilot at two clinics.
SKILLS
Product: roadmapping, A/B testing, user interviews, requirements writing
Tools: Jira, Amplitude, Excel

items.says: The résumé lacks a concise summary or target-role signal.
items.because: Readers must infer the intended direction from a non-obvious career sequence, and the current mechanic title may dominate the first impression.

items.says: The experience entries are not in reverse chronological order.
items.because: The 2024 Harbor Payments internship appears after the 2018–2023 Crestline role, making the document look mechanically inconsistent.

items.says: The résumé presents competing product, operations, and mechanical narratives without making one primary.
items.because: The reader currently has to assemble the operations-to-product story themselves.

items.says: For product applications, the section order may not surface product evidence quickly enough.
items.because: Harbor Payments, Campus Food Rescue, and other product evidence should appear quickly.

items.says: The skills section is too small and generic for product applications.
items.because: Skills should reinforce the target story rather than introduce unsupported capabilities.

items.says: The résumé relies repeatedly on “presented” and “led” without always clarifying the resulting decision or outcome.
items.because: The résumé is strongest when it shows what changed rather than simply listing activities.

items.says: Metric terminology is not standardized across the résumé.
items.because: Inconsistent distinctions among percent change, percentage points, annualized savings, time saved, and pilots can make the document look less rigorous.

items.says: The placeholder-style profile URL should be replaced with the actual public destination if it is not real.
items.because: Placeholder-looking contact information reduces credibility.

items.says: The profile link should be labeled clearly if it is a LinkedIn profile rather than a personal website.
items.because: A recruiter should know what they will find when clicking.

items.says: Consider adding the current city and state.
items.because: Employers often screen for location, relocation, or work-authorization logistics.

items.says: Add work authorization if it is relevant to the targeted roles or employers.
items.because: It can remove an early screening question.

items.says: The MBA completion status should be stated accurately and made immediately clear.
items.because: The reader should be able to tell whether the degree is completed, in progress, or recently completed.

items.says: Consider adding a directly relevant concentration, course, leadership role, or academic distinction.
items.because: A bare MBA line establishes the credential but does not distinguish the candidate from other MBA applicants.

items.says: Consider adding honors, academic distinction, or strong quantitative coursework if applicable.
items.because: The economics degree supports analytical positioning but is not currently a differentiator.

items.says: The bullet does not clarify the candidate’s personal responsibility for the rebuilds.
items.because: It is unclear whether the work was independently owned or performed as part of a team.

items.says: The bullet does not make its transferable operational value obvious to a product recruiter.
items.because: More context is needed to show ownership, prioritization, problem-solving, and delivery under hard constraints.

items.says: The bullet lacks measurable scope or a stronger operational outcome.
items.because: The maintenance work is not especially relevant to product roles, and “logged service records” is low impact without evidence of compliance, uptime, safety, turnaround, or process improvement.

items.says: The scorecard bullet lacks scale such as the number of carriers, managers, sites, or lanes covered.
items.because: The current wording underdevelops the performance-measurement and stakeholder-management signal.

items.says: The bullet does not show what decisions or achievements resulted from the scorecards and review meeting.
items.because: It reads as a recurring responsibility, and merely discussing scorecards sounds passive.

items.says: The pick-error reduction lacks a baseline or business consequence.
items.because: Rework, complaints, labor hours, or fulfillment cost would clarify the operational impact.

items.says: The bullet does not clarify the candidate’s role in designing or implementing the consensus forecast.
items.because: The review wants clearer ownership of the improvement.

items.says: The bullet does not identify which business decisions improved because of the lower forecast error.
items.because: Its effect on inventory, capacity, purchasing, service levels, or planning is not shown.

items.says: The bullet contains too many different responsibilities and should be separated or clarified.
items.because: Implementation, documentation, adoption, vendor management, and efficiency impact compete with the central achievement.

items.says: The basis for the annual 1,800-driver-hour saving is not explained.
items.because: The review asks how the saving was measured and calculated.

items.says: “Redesigned” does not establish what the candidate personally owned.
items.because: Product reviewers will want to know whether the candidate owned research, requirements, design, experimentation, implementation, or launch.

items.says: The experiment lacks context on duration, success criteria, statistical reliability, and whether the lift was sustained.
items.because: The reader needs to distinguish a robust product experiment from a temporary or noisy result.

items.says: The RICE bullet shows methodology without an adopted decision or outcome.
items.because: Merely using RICE is not a result.

items.says: The use of support tickets as the RICE Reach measure needs a rationale.
items.because: Standard RICE Reach is usually based on users, accounts, or events, although tickets can be valid in some contexts.

items.says: The bullet does not clearly show what happened after the roadmap priority was set.
items.because: It lists many activities without stating whether the priority was approved, funded, or shipped.

items.says: The bullet duplicates the checkout conversion result already reported on line 17.
items.because: Repeating the same result makes the internship look repetitive rather than comprehensive.

items.says: The session-randomization detail may be unnecessary as a separate bullet.
items.because: It is useful only when experimentation rigor is central to the target role or there is room to explain the methodology and decision.

items.says: The bullet should specify the candidate’s role in the presentation and supporting analysis.
items.because: The review wants clearer personal ownership.

items.says: The bullet does not establish whether the funding decision was directly attributable to the candidate’s analysis.
items.because: The causal connection between the work and the expansion decision needs clarification.

items.says: The bullet does not clarify whether the app was built and launched individually or by a team, or what product decisions the candidate owned.
items.because: The reader needs to understand the product’s maturity and the candidate’s personal ownership.

items.says: The measurement basis for the nine tonnes of redistributed food is not explained.
items.because: The impact figure needs clearer support.

items.says: The increase from 400 to 1,150 weekly active users is not 150%; it is 187.5%.
items.because: The incorrect percentage is an obvious numerical credibility problem.

items.says: The causal connection between the interviews, pickup reminders, and user growth needs clarification.
items.because: “Chosen after 60 user interviews” may overstate causality unless the interviews clearly identified reminders as the intervention.

items.says: The change from 75% to 95% is a 20-percentage-point increase, not a 20% relative increase.
items.because: The relative increase is 26.7%, so precision is needed.

items.says: The bullet does not explain what analysis produced the $2.4 million savings estimate.
items.because: The financial impact needs a clearer analytical basis.

items.says: The bullet does not state what portion of the recommendation the candidate personally led.
items.because: The review wants clearer ownership of the team result.

items.says: The bullet does not clarify whether the savings estimate was validated or only a theoretical opportunity.
items.because: The credibility of the projected savings depends on that distinction.

items.says: The intake-form change lacks a measurable outcome, and “adopted” is vague.
items.because: The bullet shows implementation without demonstrating reduced intake time, fewer missing fields, lower abandonment, or staff hours saved.

items.says: The pilot approval duplicates the pilot outcome already reported on line 28.
items.because: Two bullets about the same approval make the practicum section repetitive.

items.says: The roadmapping skill is not fully supported by a clear decision or outcome in the experience bullets.
items.because: Skills demonstrated through outcomes are more persuasive than skills listed alone.

items.says: Requirements writing is not clearly demonstrated elsewhere in the résumé.
items.because: A skill that appears only in the skills section is less persuasive.

items.says: The generic “Tools” list does not show proficiency or what each tool supported.
items.because: Product recruiters care more about what was accomplished with a tool than the tool name alone.

items.says: Jira is not supported by evidence of backlog, sprint, or delivery work.
items.because: Without actual-use evidence, the tool carries little weight.

items.says: Amplitude is not supported by evidence of funnel, retention, cohort, experiment, or other product analysis.
items.because: Amplitude needs to connect to product analytics to be a meaningful signal.
